newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines' Ramos pledges total success for APEC.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ramos pledges total success for APEC.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday the Philippines was aiming for total success as host of this year's Asia-Pacific summit to be attended by U.S. President Bill Clinton and other leaders of the booming region.

"We have done everything possible and we have assured the 18 member economies that everything is ready here," he told a news conference at the start of six days of meetings culminating in the summit on Monday at Subic Bay, just north of Manila.
"We want total success," he said.

Clinton, China's Jiang Zemin, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and the other leaders are coming to the Philippines to mark what officials have described as a turning point for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.

APEC, which began in 1989 as a ministerial meeting in Australia, has been dismissed by critics as nothing but a talking shop and the summit that has now become an annual rite as a mere photo opportunity.

But organisers say the Manila and Subic meetings will start to produce concrete progress towards APEC's state of dropping all trade and investment barriers in the region by 2020, turning the grouping into the world's biggest and wealthiest free trade zone.
The Philippines, fearing protests by anti-APEC leftists, has imposed strict security measures for this fourth annual APEC summit and the ministerial meeting that precedes it on Friday and Saturday.
Manila officials say the leftists are trying to stir up labour unrest and stage other protests in an attempt to embarrass the government.
A security alert involving a pipe bomb at Subic turned out to be a drill, according to Richard Gordon, chairman of the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority which runs the former U.S. naval base.
"It's a drill," he told Reuters.

The government has accused leftists of plotting to embarrass the government, which sees its role as APEC host as an opportunity to showcase its own economic recovery and to shake off its image as a place of great charm but little else.
Ramos said he hoped APEC would show the world "we are attractive, we are competitive, we are capable and that we have a contribution to make... to the Asia-Pacific economies".
The summit also provides opportunities for one-on-one meetings between leaders. Among bilaterals already announced are meetings between Clinton and Jiang and Clinton and Hashimoto.

One of its other results is likely to be a united APEC front at next month's World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting over a U.S. proposal for liberalisation in the trade in information technology products, according to organisers.

Clinton, visiting Australia on his way to the Philippines, urged fellow Asia-Pacific leaders on Wednesday to spearhead the free trade push with cuts to barriers in the one trillion dollars a year information technology industry.
Despite the Philippine government push for the Subic summit's success, APEC has not won total support in Manila.
The capital's normally impossible traffic has been made even worse by so-called "friendship lanes" from which vehicles without special passes are banished, infuriating other road-users.
Five Filipinos, also shaved their heads to demonstrate their opposition to the summit and 30 colleagues began a 24-hour fast.

"This is our way of showing what APEC will do to our country. Foreign companies will come and exploit our cheap labour and deplete our enviornment," housewife Jesusa Rebite, 30, told reporters while fellow demonstrators gave her and four male activists a crude shave with scissors and blades.
But while drivers fumed and others protested, one group of activists showered each other with flower petals, hugged and invoked the universal spirit of peace and understanding.

"If APEC is here it is because it was meant to happen," said Corazon Juliano Soliman, leading an opening ritual at Code-NGO, the main conference of anti-APEC groups who do not see free trade as a panacea and urge added protections for the poor.
